title: Learning What Evaluators Value: A Reliable Approach to Modeling Evaluator Preferences
claim: Evaluators map multiple per-criterion assessments to an overall score, in domains as different as hotel reviews and peer review.
layout: 2 stacked panels, (a) hotel reviews on top, (b) paper reviews below, side-by-side examples
description: The figure has two stacked panels of real review examples. Panel (a), 'Example Tripadvisor reviews', shows three hotel reviews side by side. Each lists six criteria (Value, Rooms, Location, Cleanliness, Service, Sleep Quality) as rows of five green circles, filled or hollow to give a 0–5 rating. Below the criteria is an 'Overall rating' in the same circle format. In the first review the overall rating is a full five circles. Panel (b), 'Example ICLR 2024 reviews', shows two text boxes with criterion scores (Soundness, Presentation, Contribution, such as '3 good' or '4 excellent') in bold dark-red labels. Below each is a Rating line, such as '8: accept, good paper'. The eye goes first to the green dot rows at the top left. The figure is clean, with a white background and no arrows.
caption: An illustration of the evaluation settings we consider. Evaluators provide criteria evaluations alongside an overall score or recommendation. Our focus is on learning how evaluators map assessments of criteria (e.g., cleanliness or soundness) to their overall scores (e.g., a stay rated 4 out of 5 stars, or a review says 8: accept).
abstract: In many applications, human and LLM evaluators use assessments of relevant criteria to create an overall evaluation for an item or individual. For example, in admissions, committees assess candidates on attributes such as test scores, GPA, and research experience to evaluate their overall fit for the program. Another example arises in medical care, where clinicians use patient reports of symptoms to consider preliminary diagnoses and assess risks. Each setting involves mapping multiple criteria to an overall evaluation---a process that reflects the evaluator's underlying preferences. We focus on the fundamental question of learning these preferences. Many applications of this problem make specific modeling assumptions on evaluator preferences that may be substantially violated in the real world. We make the minimal assumption that the preference function is coordinate-wise non-decreasing, which is reasonable in a large number of evaluation settings. We theoretically characterize the severity of model mismatch for many common assumptions and show that it can lead to significant issues for learning evaluator preferences and other important downstream tasks. We then present an algorithm for learning evaluators' preferences that is robust to model mismatch. We prove theoretically that our algorithm can learn any preference function without sacrificing performance when the linearity assumption holds. Evaluations of our algorithm with synthetic simulations and real-world data confirm its ability to learn preferences robustly and illustrate key aspects of LLM and human preferences. To conclude, we present a case study of how to use our method to provide insights into reviewer preferences and increase fairness in the peer review process.
